title: Bidirectional Variability in Measured Pelvic Incidence After Posterior Long-Segment Fusion for Adult Spinal Deformity
content: Objective: Pelvic incidence (PI) is generally considered a fixed morphologic parameter after skeletal maturity, although postoperative variation has been reported following spinal fusion. This study examined whether measured PI changes after posterior long-segment fusion for adult spinal deformity, with particular emphasis on bidirectional variability at the patient level. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent posterior fusion across at least five levels between 2010 and 2015. Two independent observers measured preoperative and postoperative spinopelvic parameters on standing full-length spine radiographs, and the mean of their PI measurements was used in the analyses. Interobserver agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Patients were grouped according to whether the distal construct terminated in the lumbar spine or extended to the pelvis. Because no prespecified direction of postoperative PI change was assumed, both the directional change and the absolute patient-level difference were analyzed. Results: The study included 42 patients, 38 of whom were women. Mean age was 69.64 ± 6.94 years, and median follow-up was 42.5 months (interquartile range [IQR], 26–59 months). Mean PI increased from 49.6 ± 11.97° preoperatively to 52.5 ± 10.01° postoperatively (p = 0.097), corresponding to a mean directional change of 2.94 ± 11.20°. Directional changes also did not reach statistical significance within either distal-fusion subgroup. The median absolute PI difference was 6° (IQR, 2–13.5°; p < 0.001). Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and back- and leg-pain visual analog scale (VAS) scores decreased significantly after surgery (all p < 0.001), but the magnitude of these changes was not correlated with PI variability. Interobserver agreement ranged from moderate to good (ICC, 0.715–0.857). Conclusion: Measured PI varied in both directions after posterior long-segment fusion. The mean directional shift was small, and the observed magnitude should be interpreted in the context of radiographic measurement variability. PI variability was not associated with changes in disability or pain scores and may reflect postoperative spinopelvic adaptation rather than symptomatic recovery. Reassessment of the current spinopelvic profile may be useful during long-term follow-up and revision planning.
